notes:
I've put together notes for all 21 verses, but the coverage isn't even. Most of it comes from Enduring Word (David Guzik), the older commentaries on StudyLight and BibleHub (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Gill, Barnes, Calvin, Spurgeon, Keil & Delitzsch) and the NET Bible notes.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on the Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal, Catholic or Orthodox sites, and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out as you asked. I also tried to open Matthew Henry's full commentary on Isaiah 26, but the page came back without the commentary text.

## Introduction
- **Where the chapter sits:** BibleHub's Q&A page calls Isaiah 24–27 a prophetic "little apocalypse." Isaiah 26 is a hymn of trust celebrating God's future deliverance of His covenant people. https://biblehub.com/q/Isaiah_26_19_and_bodily_resurrection.htm
- **When "that day" is:** The readings split over this.
  - Guzik says the context from Isaiah 24-25 points to the day of the Messiah's ultimate triumph. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
  - The Geneva Study Bible says this song was made to comfort the faithful when their captivity would come, assuring them also of their deliverance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-1.htm
  - Matthew Henry reads "that day" as the gospel day, which the day of the victories and enlargements of the Old-Testament church was typical of. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_026.cfm
- **A historical setting:** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary connects the song to Jerusalem's escape from Assyria. Judah had been marvellously protected from the invading Assyrian. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-26.html

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik uses Augustine's language: the strong city is the Kingdom of God, the city of man is the world system. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Ellicott says the walls of the heavenly city are not of stone or brick, but are themselves as a living force, saving and protecting. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-1.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes the city as Jerusalem, a strong city because God protects it, and a picture of the New Jerusalem. They argue the context cannot admit of the restoration from Babylon under Cyrus being its ultimate and exhaustive fulfillment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian) points out that the city wasn't heavily fortified at the time. Its strength would come from Yahweh would be a protector. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the city is only for the righteous, and those who keep the truth. In the same principle, the New Jerusalem is a city filled with glory, which excludes the unrighteous. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown identifies the "righteous nation" as the godly remnant that had not apostatized during the captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) turns the verse into an invitation to come in: the Son of David has set before us an open door, and no man can shut it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-26.html

**v. 3**
- **"Perfect peace":** In Hebrew this is "shalom shalom." Guzik notes that in Hebrew, repetition communicates intensity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/ Ellicott makes the same point: completeness is expressed, as elsewhere, in the form of iteration. No adjectives can add to the fulness of the meaning of the noun. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/26-3.htm
- **"Stayed":** Guzik says the Hebrew word means to prop up, lean on or be sustained. A mind that only occasionally leans on the Lord is not enough; it has to be stayed on Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Spurgeon stresses that God is the one who gives the peace: it is God Himself that can give us this peace, and keep us in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-26.html
- **A Reformed emphasis:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reports that Calvin reads the phrase as "(In thy) firm decree (or purpose) thou keepest (the Church) in perfect peace." On that reading, the Church's peace does not depend on the state of the world, nor upon our wandering purposes, but upon the fixed purpose and immutable counsel of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- **A Catholic translation difference:** The Douay-Rheims Bible translates the verse quite differently: The old error is passed away: thou wilt keep peace: peace, because we have hoped in thee. I found no Catholic commentary explaining this wording. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/26-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik says the Lord gives the mind a reason to trust him: It isn't that the LORD has everlasting strength, He is everlasting strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Hebrew is literally "the rock of ages," and that the union of the two names expresses in the highest degree God's unchanging love and power. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**vv. 5–6**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes the lofty city as Babylon; representative of the stronghold of the foes of God's people in all ages. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Guzik sees a reversal. The city of man is built on the backs of the weak and the poor. But when God brings the city of man down to the dust, He will turn all that around. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/

**v. 7**
- Guzik says the order matters: the LORD makes His people just by a relationship of faith and trust in Him, then they walk in the way of…uprightness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, following Calvin, says the prophet is not praising the just, but is showing that God gives a prosperous issue to their course, however rugged it may seem for a time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 8**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads the waiting as waiting for God to punish the enemy. They take "Your name" to mean the manifested character of God by which He would be remembered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Guzik says desire shows itself in waiting, and in seeking God early and at night. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/

**v. 9**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes "the people of the world" to mean the nations left after judgments shall have been executed. They add that deliverance follows prayer by God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: The wicked are ungrateful for God's goodness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says that when the wicked prosper alongside the just, the wicked don't learn righteousness. That is why judgments have to be sent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 11**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Lowth's translation, 'they shall see with confusion thy zeal for thy people.' They read the fire as the fire of thy vengeance, to which thine enemies are doomed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik links this verse to Ephesians 2:8–10: Even our good works are works that He has done…in us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- **A grammar point to know before preaching "in us":** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Hebrew is the same word in both halves of the verse. The seeming antithesis of for and in is unreal. Both ought to be "for us." The BSB already reads "for us." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 13**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown reads the "other lords" two ways. They are earthly rulers such as Nebuchadnezzar, and also idols and lusts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Guzik: The humble heart repents of past idolatry, and rejoices in the present freedom in the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/

**v. 14**
- Ellicott takes "the dead" to be the rulers of the great world-empires, who went down to the world of the dead with no way out. He also notes that the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) read the word for "spirits" (Hebrew *rephaim*) differently: "Physicians shall not raise them up to life." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-14.htm
- Barnes explains that "rephaim" was a name given to the shades or manes of the dead, from an idea that they were weak and powerless. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-14.htm
- Coffman quotes the Broadman Bible Commentary (Baptist): "The meaning of Isaiah 26:14 is that the death of the wicked will be final and irrevocable… they will never rise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-14.html

**v. 15**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the past tense a prophetic preterite: something future described as if already done. They prefer the translation "thou hast extended far all the borders of the land." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html

**v. 16**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Hebrew word for prayer means a whisper, a secret sighing to God for help. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: Before, prayer came drop by drop; now they pour it out, it comes now like water from a fountain. Afflictions bring us to secret prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-14.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls childbirth an image of anguish accompanied with expectation. They see a contrast with verse 19: what we vainly attempt, God will accomplish. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- Guzik: The humble heart knows the futility of working apart from the direction and blessing of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/

**v. 19 (the most debated verse)**
- **Literal bodily resurrection:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary sees here only a resurrection of the just, perhaps only of the just Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html
  - Another commentator quoted on BibleHub's commentary page compares it with Ezekiel's vision of dry bones and says there can be no doubt that here a literal resurrection of individuals is foretold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/26-19.htm
  - Coffman criticises Barnes' national reading as totally inadequate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html
- **Mainly about the nation being restored:**
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) says the people had been dead; that is, civilly dead in Babylon. He adds that the imagery still implies that that doctrine was one with which they were familiar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/isaiah/26-19.html
  - Ellicott (Anglican) sees it as primarily used of national and spiritual resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html
- **Both meanings:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it means first a spiritual and national restoration, but ultimately, and in the fullest scope of the prophecy, they shall be restored to life literally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
- **"My dead body" read as Christ's body:**
  - Gill (Baptist) says as sure as Christ's dead body was raised, so sure shall everyone of his people be raised. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n95/isaiah/26-19.html
  - Calvin (Reformed) takes it as the prophet counting himself among the dead who will rise, provided he is part of the Church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html
- **A Calvary Chapel reading:** Chuck Smith links the verse to the saints who rose in Matthew 27:52–53 and says this particular verse is a prophecy that is making reference to that event. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/26-19.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes):** It is not certain whether the resurrection envisioned here is intended to be literal or figurative. A comparison with 25:8 and Dan 12:2 suggests a literal interpretation, but Ezek 37:1-14 uses resurrection as a metaphor for deliverance from exile. On the "dew," the notes add that dew is a symbol of fertility and life. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=isa&chapter=26&verse=19

**v. 20 (real disagreement over the rapture)**
- **Pre-Tribulation rapture (Calvary Chapel):**
  - Guzik admits the verse could refer to the deliverance of the Jewish people from the fury of the Antichrist. But he thinks it more likely means believers caught up to meet the Lord. He concludes it is a powerful passage supporting the teaching of the Pre-Tribulation Rapture. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
  - Chuck Smith reads "the indignation" as the Great Tribulation. He adds that those who hold a post-Tribulation view get no comfort, no pleasure, no joy out of that verse of scripture. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bis/isaiah/26-20.html
- **God sheltering his people in history (Presbyterian and older readings):**
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown compares it to God shutting Noah in, Israel staying indoors at the Passover, a Zoar for Lot in the destruction of Sodom, and a Pella for Christians in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
  - The Geneva Bible says he exhorts the faithful to be patient in their afflictions and to wait on God's work. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bis/isaiah/26-20.html
  - Matthew Henry notes that verses 20–21 are supposed not to belong to the song and may introduce chapter 27 instead. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_026.cfm

**v. 21**
- Guzik points out that this wrath is from the LORD Himself. This is not persecution from the wicked, but judgment from the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-26/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links it to Abel's blood crying out (Genesis 4:10): All the innocent blood shed, and all other wrongs done, so long seemingly with impunity, shall then be avenged. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/isaiah-26.html
